top_cited_works.title: The Many Faces of Turbine Surface Roughness
top_cited_works.abstract: Results are presented for contact stylus measurements of surface roughness on in-service turbine blades and vanes. Nearly 100 turbine components were assembled from four land-based turbine manufacturers. Both coated and uncoated, cooled and uncooled components were measured, with part sizes varying from 2 to 20 cm. Spanwise and chordwise two-dimensional roughness profiles were taken on both pressure and suction surfaces. Statistical computations were performed on each trace to determine centerline averaged roughness, rms roughness, and peak to-valley height. In addition, skewness and kurtosis were calculated; as well as the autocorrelation length and dominant harmonics in each trace. Extensive three-dimensional surface maps made of deposits, pitting, erosion, and coating spallation expose unique features for each roughness type. Significant spatial variations are evidenced and transitions from rough to smooth surface conditions are shown to be remarkably abrupt in some cases. Film cooling sites are shown to be particularly prone to surface degradation.

top_cited_works.title: Effect of Density Ratio on Flat Plate Film Cooling With Shaped Holes Using PSP
top_cited_works.abstract: Detailed film-cooling effectiveness distributions are obtained on a flat plate using the pressure sensitive paint (PSP) technique. The applicability of the PSP technique is expanded to include a coolant-to-mainstream density ratio of 1.4. The effect of density ratio on the film-cooling effectiveness is coupled with varying blowing ratio (M=0.25–2.0), freestream turbulence intensity (Tu=1–12.5%), and film hole geometry. The effectiveness distributions are obtained on three separate flat plates containing either simple angle, cylindrical holes, simple angle, fanshaped holes (α=10 deg), or simple angle, laidback, fanshaped holes (α=10 deg and γ=10 deg). In all three cases, the film-cooling holes are angled at θ=35 deg from the mainstream flow. Using the PSP technique, the combined effects of blowing ratio, turbulence intensity, and density ratio are captured for each film-cooling geometry. top_cited_works.title: Uncertainty analysis of metal-casting porosity measurements using Archimedes' principle
top_cited_works.venue: International Journal of Cast Metals Research
top_cited_works.abstract: A detailed uncertainty-analysis model is developed for metal-casting porosity measurement using Archimedes' principle. The model is used to investigate the influence of liquid density on the sensitivity coefficients in the uncertainty propagation equation. The sensitivity coefficients are found to be very large, resulting in significant magnification of uncertainties in weight measurements and liquid and theoretical density estimates. Increasing the density of the liquid results in a decrease in sensitivity coefficients and an improvement in porosity accuracy. A numerical example is given to demonstrate the process of estimating the measurement uncertainties and typical uncertainties that can be expected in metal-casting porosity measurements.

recent_works.title: Roughness and Scallop Analyses of the IPW2 CRM65 Midspan Hybrid Model Extra Cases
recent_works.abstract: The AIAA Ice Prediction Workshop series provides icing researchers with a common set of ice accretion measurements from various icing wind tunnels that are used to compare and improve 2D and 3D ice accretion prediction codes and simulation methodologies. As part of the 2nd Ice Prediction Workshop, a set of “Extra Cases” measured in the Icing Research Tunnel at NASA Glenn Research Center was provided that enables an investigation of roughness and scallop time evolution with ice accretion times ranging from 2.5 minutes to 29 minutes. The conditions of the additional cases are closely related to the “Max Scallop” case on the CRM65 Midspan Hybrid model but with a different angle of attack and flap deflection. While the stronger circulation of the Max Scallop case is not present, the ice shapes of the Extra Cases contain features that appear to be scallops. In this investigation, the self-organizing map approach of McClain and Kreeger (2013) and the voxelization and autocorrelation approach of McClain (2022) are used to characterize the time evolution of the roughness and scallop features of the Extra Cases. recent_works.title: Collection Efficiency Measurements Using Linear Microstrip Sensors and Blotting Media
recent_works.abstract: The use of surface-mounted microstrip sensors for the measurement of water collection using flexible printed circuit boards and microwave group delay analyses has been demonstrated in recent investigations. In the most recent study by McClain et al. (2025), the sensors were employed in “direct” operating mode as opposed to use with a blotting media similar to the dye-capture approach of Papadakis (2007). In the present work, the 9-in. NACA 0012 model of McClain et al. (2025) was employed with cotton capture media attached to the model. The benefit of using the blotting media is that the water drops are held in place following capture until the media begins to saturate. In the direct operating mode, only a very short operating time is available to acquire measurements before the beads that collect on an airfoil surface begin to run back along the surface. recent_works.title: Frost Thickness and Roughness Evolution on Cold-Soaked, Fuel-Laden Wings
recent_works.abstract: Frost that forms on the surface of wings with fuel remaining in integrated fuel tanks following a flight is referred to as cold soaked fuel frost. Frost roughness was characterized using two experimental facilities which provided different methods for capturing the thermodynamic environment representing the cold soaked fuel frost growth process. A photogrammetric approach was developed to measure frost roughness and used in each facility. Modeling approaches were developed to predict the evolution of cold-soaked fuel frost roughness characteristics.

recent_works.title: Microwave Sensing of Water Accumulation using a Microstrip Line
recent_works.abstract: In aviation, water collection efficiency describes the proportion of liquid water droplets in the airflow that impinge on an aircraft’s surface while flying through clouds or precipitation. This parameter is essential for icing analysis because it determines how much water can freeze on critical components such as wings and engine inlets. Traditional measurement approaches, such as the dye-water blotter-medium method developed by Papadakis et al. (M. Papadakis, S.-C. Wong, A. Rachman, K. E. Hung, G. T. Vu, and C. S. Bidwell, “Large and small droplet impingement data on airfoils and two simulated ice shapes,” NASA Technical Memorandum NASA/TM-2007-213959, Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA, Oct. 1, 2007.), provided valuable insights but suffered from key limitations: the measurement is time-consuming and challenging to implement, and the system required a specially designed spray bar system for implementation in NASA icing wind tunnels.
